tool_name: Height — 'autonomous' project management tool that combined tasks, chat, docs, and AI agents (Copilot) in a single workspace. Vendor: Height Labs, Inc. (height.app). Founded 2018, publicly available from late 2021. Shut down on September 24, 2025; the product is referenced here historically because its task+chat setup model influenced an entire generation of AI-native PM tools.
target_user: Individual contributors and team leads — fully self-service. The signup flow was designed for a founder, PM, or engineering lead to create a workspace, import their backlog, invite teammates, and start collaborating without IT involvement. There is no notion of a central admin gate for team creation. Workspace admin existed for billing, SSO, and integration installation, but setup itself was a single-person action. The dominant persona was a small product/engineering team (5–50) at a startup or scale-up.
setup_time_estimate: Minutes to a working list, hours to a comfortable workflow. Reviewers consistently described onboarding as 'smooth and well-guided, with teams becoming productive within the first week' (Vact, copy.ai). One review framed it as 'the fastest PM tool onboarding after Trello' — initial setup 'takes less time than configuring a single Asana project.' The 0.105 release (blog post 'Import tasks in onboarding and paging in chat') explicitly moved Jira Cloud and CSV import into the onboarding flow itself, so a team could land with their existing backlog already in place rather than starting empty. [uncertain] No vendor-published median time-to-first-sprint metric was found.
onboarding_wizard: Yes — a guided first-run flow that combined workspace creation, sample data, and import in one path. Steps observed in reviews and the Height changelog: create account → name workspace → create first list (the unit of work organization) → create first task → invite team → optionally import from Jira Cloud or CSV → optionally enable Copilot AI features. There was no Scrum/Kanban/SAFe framework picker — Height was opinionated about lists+tasks+chat rather than ceremony-specific scaffolding. The onboarding-time Jira/CSV importer was added in release 0.105 specifically to remove the 'empty workspace' cliff, letting users land with hundreds of existing tasks already present. Automation templates were surfaced inside onboarding to reduce the moderate learning curve for setting up workflows.
template_library: Two templating mechanisms, both self-service. (1) Template Lists — any list could be saved and reused to kickstart a new project (new-hire onboarding, marketing campaign, release plan, etc.). Templates were workspace-scoped and shareable across teams within the workspace. (2) Task Forms — schema-style templates that enforced required attributes, optional questions, and pre-linked subtasks so tasks were always created with the right context (used heavily for bug intake, design requests, customer feedback). Automation templates were also offered to soften the workflow-automation learning curve. There was no marketplace gallery comparable to Notion or ClickUp — the library was small and curated rather than crowdsourced.
ai_assisted_setup: Substantial, branded as Height Copilot. Copilot was positioned as 'the first and only AI project manager' and was active from the moment a workspace was created. Setup-relevant Copilot behaviors: (a) Smart Task Creation — type a high-level task and Copilot suggested subtasks, owners, labels, priorities within seconds; (b) Duplicate Task Prevention — flagged near-duplicates during creation so the backlog didn't bloat at import time; (c) Auto-categorisation — Copilot suggested which list a new task belonged in and applied labels; (d) Automated Standups / Status — generated daily team summaries from chat+task activity without configuration; (e) Conversation Summaries — let new joiners catch up on missed task discussions. Copilot did not auto-generate the workspace structure (lists, members, integrations), but it removed most of the manual triage and categorisation work that normally accumulates in the first weeks after setup.
hierarchy_config: Deliberately flat and flexible. The model was Workspace → List → Task → Subtask, with no enforced Portfolio/Epic/Feature layer. Lists were 'flexible containers' that could represent a project, product, feature, department, client, or virtual team. Lists had no hierarchy — all sat at the same level in the left sidebar (no nested folders). Tasks supported arbitrary custom attributes, endless cascading subtasks, and could be created directly from chat messages. Setup time for the hierarchy was effectively 'as long as it takes to name a list.' There was no SAFe-style ART/Program Increment construct; for organizations that needed multi-level rollup, this was a known gap.
multi_team_setup: Designed to scale by adding lists and inviting more people into the same workspace, not by introducing program-level structure. A workspace could hold many lists, and lists could be public to the workspace or private to specific members/guests. There was no first-class concept of teams-of-teams, ARTs, or program-level rollup. For organizations of 5–50 people in one workspace the model held up; reviewers flagged that at the multi-hundred-person scale the flat list hierarchy and absence of program-layer governance was the limiting factor. [uncertain] No specific case studies of Height at 100+ teams found.
admin_dependency: Minimal. Workspace creation, list creation, task creation, automation setup, template list creation, task form creation, and team invitations were all member-level actions. Workspace admin was required only for: SSO/SAML configuration, workspace-wide billing, installing the Slack/GitHub apps at workspace scope, and bulk member provisioning. The chat-and-task-together model removed an entire class of admin work that exists in tool-stacked competitors — e.g. no need for an IT-side Slack-Jira bridge configuration, because the chat thread on a task was native, not a federated integration.
permissions_model: Lean and member-friendly. Roles existed at the workspace level (admin / member / guest), and lists could be marked public (everyone in the workspace), private (named members only), or read-only via secret link (for clients and external reviewers). Guests could be invited to specific lists or tasks without seeing the rest of the workspace. There was no per-task ACL matrix or field-level permissioning — by design. Reviewers occasionally flagged the simplicity as a gap for highly regulated organizations, but it was almost never cited as a blocker for the startup/scale-up segment Height targeted.
import_capabilities: Self-service and present in the onboarding flow itself. Native importers shipped for Jira Cloud and CSV, both wired into the onboarding wizard (release 0.105 — 'Import tasks in onboarding and paging in chat'). CSV import accepted the standard exports from Asana, Trello, Notion, and Linear when shaped into Height's column model. Field mapping was opinionated — Jira issue types and statuses were mapped to Height's flexible task attributes rather than recreating arbitrary Jira schemes. Reviewers consistently praised the in-onboarding import as the moment that 'made the tool stick' because day-1 wasn't an empty workspace. [uncertain] Specific support for Rally / Azure DevOps / ADO import — no documentation found; CSV was the documented escape hatch.
migration_story: Customer-led, no professional-services requirement. The Hacker News thread from January 2025 ('this happens after I've moved everything to height') captured the broader pattern — small teams self-migrated from Jira/Asana/Trello in a single sitting, with the in-onboarding importer carrying the heavy lifting. The painful migration story was the reverse one in 2025: after the March 22 shutdown announcement, customers had six months to migrate OFF Height, and the ecosystem of 'best alternatives after Height shutdown' content (Kanbanchi, Shortcut, The Digital Project Manager) became the dominant migration narrative. No vendor PS engagement was ever required for either direction.
vcs_integration_setup: Self-service install, member-level configuration after install. GitHub: Workspace admin installs the Height GitHub app once at the workspace level; thereafter individual lists/tasks could be linked to repositories, branches, or PRs by any member. Height supported bi-directional PR linking — opening a PR with a Height task ID in the title auto-linked the task and updated its status on merge. GitLab and Bitbucket were also supported. Time-to-first-linked-PR was on the order of minutes after the workspace app install. [uncertain] Exact granularity of repo-level vs workspace-level scope for GitHub permissions was not explicitly documented in available sources.
slack_notifications_setup: Self-service after the one-time workspace install. Slack integration supported per-channel notifications and a slash command for creating Height tasks from any Slack message. Crucially, because Height had its own native chat tied to tasks, many Height teams used Slack only for cross-team announcements and used Height chat for in-task discussion — reducing the volume of Slack configuration needed. Any member could route channel notifications for lists they had access to; admin was only required to install the Slack app at the workspace level.
first_impression_ux: On day 1 the user landed in a clean, dark-mode-friendly UI with a default workspace, a sidebar of flat lists, a global inbox, a task view, and a persistent chat panel. The empty state did not stay empty for long — Copilot proactively suggested first tasks and the onboarding flow encouraged Jira/CSV import to populate real data. Reviewers across freshvanroot, TechRepublic, and copy.ai singled out the first impression as 'beautiful, intuitive, and fast' with an aesthetic closer to Linear/Things 3 than to Jira/Asana. The standout day-1 sensation was the chat panel: opening a task and seeing a threaded conversation already attached, rather than having to click out to Slack, was the differentiating moment.
time_to_value: Same session. Minimum viable setup was: create workspace → import Jira/CSV (or skip and create a list manually) → create a task → invite teammates → start chatting on a task. Value was felt within minutes because the chat was native — the very first task discussion already lived next to the work. The free plan was generous (unlimited members, unlimited guests, unlimited tasks/subtasks), so a team could prove value before any paid commitment. Paid tiers gated automations volume (100–2,500 automations/member/month depending on plan) and advanced Copilot features.
setup_complaints: Three recurring themes from TechRepublic, freshvanroot, copy.ai, and Hacker News reviews: (1) Moderate learning curve once the user moved past tasks into automations and Copilot configuration — Height shipped automation templates partly to mitigate this. (2) Knowledge base / documentation was 'not as extensive as other similar tools' (TechRepublic), so non-obvious behaviors required trial and error. (3) The flat list model felt great at small scale but did not give larger organizations a natural place for Portfolio/Program/ART rollup. After March 2025 the overwhelming complaint became the shutdown itself — Hacker News commenters explicitly said 'this happens after I've moved everything to height,' capturing the trust cost of platform discontinuation.
setup_praise: Recurring praise: 'beautiful, intuitive, and fast' (TechRepublic), 'onboarding experience was smooth and well-guided, with teams becoming productive within the first week' (Vact), 'takes less time than configuring a single Asana project' (copy.ai). The single most-cited 'wow' moment in reviews was the chat-on-task model — being able to discuss a task in context without context-switching to Slack was repeatedly named as the reason teams chose Height. Reviewers also praised Copilot's smart task creation: 'create a high-level task and watch Height suggest subtasks within seconds.' The aesthetic and keyboard-driven feel were grouped with Linear as the modern PM 'feel.'
standout_setup_feature: The combined task+chat model collapsed an entire class of setup work that exists in every other PM tool. Where Jira/Asana/ClickUp users have to set up a Slack bridge, configure which events post to which channel, decide where decisions are recorded, and accept that conversation lives in one tool while work lives in another, Height users started with chat already attached to every task. This reduced the 'human handoff' problem at setup time: a new teammate didn't need to be told 'discuss work in Slack, track work in the PM tool' — both lived in the same surface. The differentiating moment was opening a fresh task on day 1 and seeing a thread there waiting, with Copilot already summarising activity.
servicenow_comparison: [uncertain] No published case study found of an enterprise migrating between ServiceNow EAP and Height in either direction — Height's customer base was overwhelmingly startup/scale-up, not the SAFe-enterprise segment EAP serves. Inferred contrast: Height was the polar opposite of EAP on setup axes — chat-and-tasks-together vs ITSM-platform-with-PM-bolted-on, flat lists vs SAFe hierarchy, member-self-service vs admin-gated, free tier with unlimited tasks vs enterprise procurement. The relevant lesson for EAP is structural rather than competitive: Height proved that embedding communication directly into the work artifact eliminates a whole category of integration setup, and that AI-assisted task creation can compress the first-week 'cold start' meaningfully.
